The $3 Billion AT&T-Corning Deal Reveals an '80% Reduction in Field Splicing' for Fiber Optic Deployment | Reading the Market #39
Even if fiber optic production is increased, if the work of connecting them in the field increases at the same rate, the goal of 60 million locations will not be reached. As connections are moved to the factory, business opportunities shift from cable volume to pre-termination, inspection, and construction design.
On October 2, Furukawa Electric and Fujikura saw their stock prices rise. The catalyst was a multi-year contract worth over $3 billion signed between AT&T and Corning in the U.S. When one hears of large-scale supply of fiber optics and cables, the focus naturally turns to production capacity expansion. However, for AT&T to deliver fiber optic lines to over 60 million locations by 2030, it must also reduce the time spent connecting each line at the installation site.
1 | Even with a $3 billion contract, supply volume alone does not open lines
AT&T and Corning announced a multi-year contract worth over $3 billion on September 29. Corning will supply the fiber optics and cables necessary for network expansion.
In the Japanese market on October 2, following a significant rise in U.S. Corning stock, buying interest gathered in wire and cable stocks such as Furukawa Electric and Fujikura.
Fiber optic lines are not products that are completed just by transporting cables to a region. They are opened by branching from the trunk line to city blocks, pulling them into homes and businesses, and completing connections and loss measurements. Even if production is increased, the constraints of fusion splicing technicians and construction time remain.
AT&T reached 38.6 million locations with fiber optic lines as of the end of June 2026, and aims for over 60 million locations by the end of 2030. The simple difference is at least 21.4 million locations.
To bridge this gap, the number of hours it takes to open one location becomes critical.
2 | The number of field splices determines the expansion speed
Fusion splicing involves preparing the end face of the optical fiber, aligning the axes, and integrating them through electrical discharge. While it is low-loss and strong, it requires coating removal, cleaning, cutting, reinforcement, and loss verification.
As the number of branch points and subscriber locations increases, the total workload expands.
One countermeasure is a method where branch positions and terminals are incorporated into the cable at the factory, then terminated, sealed, and inspected before shipping. The field work then focuses on installation and terminal connection. Instead of eliminating the work, it is moved to a factory equipped with the necessary facilities and quality control.
Corning states that its 'FlexNAP' system for FTTH, which uses this method, can reduce the number of locations requiring field fusion splicing by up to 80% and the total number of splices by up to 70% compared to conventional methods. It is a configuration that incorporates factory-terminated and factory-tested access points into the distribution cable.
It has not been publicly announced that FlexNAP will be used in this AT&T contract. The 80% figure is treated as a public example showing a technical path to reducing field work.
3 | The core specification is the number of field splice points per subscriber location
The specification to watch is the number of field splice points required to open one subscriber location.
If the number of splice points per subscriber location does not change, construction personnel will be required in proportion to the deployment volume. If the work can be shifted to factory termination, the number of locations a single construction crew can open in a day can be increased.
This specification is not determined solely by the speed of the fusion splicer. It is determined by the wiring design, such as the trunk branch positions, the units where terminals are placed, the number of tethers attached at the factory, and the room for adjustment in the field.
If field fusion splicing is reduced too much, it becomes difficult to respond to changes in road shapes or house locations. The more the scope determined at the factory is expanded, the heavier the design information and part number management become. The 80% maximum is a figure that represents both work reduction and the shifting of responsibility to the factory.
4 | Moving connections to the factory changes the work that increases
Splicing remains for trunk connections, repairs, and exceptional routes. What increases is connector termination at the factory, sealing of branch points, end-face inspection, insertion loss measurement, cable identification, and verification of installation locations.
Furukawa Electric handles optical fibers, cables, connection components, fusion splicers, and testers, and is strengthening its North American sales structure. Fujikura also develops everything from fibers to fusion splicers, connectors, and cleaners.
It cannot be confirmed that both companies are participating in the AT&T contract. When North American optical lines shift from 'bulk cable + field splicing' to 'factory-terminated wiring + connection/inspection,' I want to investigate which of our company's product numbers can enter the design stage.
Unless it reaches access network design, construction standards, and field operations, the number of splicing points cannot be changed.
5 | Dividing 21.4 million locations into addressable markets
The exact addressable market is unknown.
The over $3 billion is the total contract amount for optical fiber and cable, not the market value for pre-terminated components, fusion splicers, testers, and construction. The difference between 38.6 million and over 60 million locations, at least 21.4 million locations, also includes acquired networks and open access portions, and not everything is newly built or made by Corning.
To get closer to the project scale, we accumulate by region: number of new locations × number of terminals/connectors per location × adoption unit price. Equipment is estimated from the number of cable product numbers terminated at the factory, the number of assembly lines, and the number of stations for end-face inspection and loss measurement.
Corning states that FlexNAP often saves $25 in field labor per home. A simple application to all 21.4 million locations would be $535 million, but this is not product sales. It is necessary to confirm and reduce based on target regions, wiring methods, existing equipment, and adoption rates.
6 | Ask those who decide specifications about the remaining splicing
AT&T's access network design determines the branch configuration, and construction standards and field operations evaluate work time and repairability. Corning's product design, production technology, and quality assurance concretize the loss, sealing, identification, and shipping inspection of factory-terminated parts.
First, I would like to confirm the following.
'Until one subscriber point is opened, how many field splices are currently required, and how many of them can be moved to factory termination?'
Continuing, I will confirm the remaining connection points, end-face cleaning/inspection, redesign during route changes, replacement units during failures, and design freeze dates.
Projects with high value to pursue are those where the region and annual number of locations are decided, and where technicians or construction time constrain expansion. If the amount of new construction is small, the inventory burden of increasing product numbers is large, or approved configurations cannot be changed, the priority is lowered.
The over $3 billion contract between AT&T and Corning indicated large-scale demand. However, the work of deploying to over 60 million locations by 2030 does not end with just making glass.
Reduce field splicing and move connections to factory termination. Demand leads to pre-terminated cables, branch terminals, sealing, end-face inspection, loss measurement, and construction data. The specification of up to an 80% reduction connects field personnel numbers with factory quality control.
If investigating from tomorrow, I will track AT&T's new location counts by region, the number of field splices in conventional configurations, connection points that can be moved to factory termination, design freeze dates, and construction company approval conditions.
If you are in sales, do not ask, "Will demand for optical fiber increase?" Instead, ask, "Regarding your annual activation targets, which field splicing tasks are limiting the number of jobs your installation crews can handle?" Once you have the answer, you can propose your company's materials, components, and equipment based on the labor time that can be saved, rather than just the volume of cable.
Thank you for reading until the end.
It encourages me to write more good articles, so if you found this even slightly interesting, I would appreciate your support by following and clicking the 'Like' button.

Corning wins over $3bn AT&T fiber deal on data demand
By Martin Holloway29/09/2026No Comments4 Mins Read
Corning (GLW) has landed an AT&T fiber deal worth more than $3bn, the two companies said on 29 September 2026. AT&T will procure fibre and cable from Corning under a multi-year supply agreement, as first reported by Reuters.
Corning shares climbed 4.01% to $157.60 by 16:00 UTC on the day of the announcement, having risen 3.3% in premarket trading, according to Reuters. The move came despite the stock sitting 6.07% below its 20-day range ahead of the news.
An AT&T fiber deal that dwarfs the 2024 tie-up
GLW over the last month, hourly closes. Source: consolidated US exchange data.
Neither company disclosed the contract’s exact duration or annual value. But the new agreement marks a sharp escalation from a prior AT&T-Corning fibre commitment of more than $1bn struck in 2024, according to Converge Digest. Broadband Breakfast reported that terms beyond the headline figure were withheld by both parties, a gap that leaves the near-term revenue cadence for Corning’s optical business unclear.
AT&T pointed to data volumes as the driver. The average AT&T Fibre household now uses more than one terabyte of data a month, five times the level in 2016, Reuters reported, with usage expected to keep rising as AI, cloud and streaming traffic grows.
Fibre build-out fits a wider spending push
The deal sits inside a much larger AT&T infrastructure programme. The carrier has committed more than $250bn over five years to strengthen US connectivity, and it closed a $5.75bn acquisition of Lumen’s fibre business to extend its network footprint, per Reuters. AT&T has said the build-out supports a goal of bringing fast, reliable internet to 60 million Americans by the end of 2030, according to the companies’ joint release carried by PR Newswire.
For Corning, the contract lands as its earnings recover from a volatile patch. Net income swung from a loss of $117m in the third quarter of 2024 to $559m in the second quarter of 2026, according to filings with the SEC. Diluted earnings per share over the same run moved from a 14-cent loss to 64 cents. Against that backdrop, a supply commitment north of $3bn — even spread across several years — represents a meaningful anchor for the optical communications division.
No sign of a pre-announcement short squeeze
Corning Inc /Ny revenue by quarter, as filed. Source: SEC EDGAR.
Trading data show no unusual positioning ahead of the news. Corning’s short-sale ratio, tracked by FINRA, moved between roughly 0.35 and 0.52 in the ten sessions to 28 September, in line with its recent range rather than spiking as the deal took shape. That suggests the share reaction reflected the announcement itself rather than any leak or pre-positioning by short sellers.
The Wall Street Journal separately confirmed the more-than-$3bn valuation in its own report on the tie-up, adding to a run of same-day coverage that left the core numbers uncontested even as duration and per-year terms stayed private.
The open question for investors is cadence: how the $3bn-plus commitment breaks down year by year, and how much of it lands in Corning’s results before 2030. Neither company has set a date for further disclosure, and the next scheduled data point is Corning’s following quarterly filing with the SEC, where any change in backlog or customer concentration tied to AT&T would typically surface first.
Until then, the market has taken the headline number at face value. Corning’s shares closed the announcement session near the top of their recent trading band, with the stock’s 20-day high sitting at $170.00 — a level traders will watch if fresh detail on the AT&T contract emerges.

Jim Cramer remained positive on Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) during Mad Money on October 1, despite acknowledging that it was among the previous quarter's S&P 500 weakest stocks. He said:
On the first day of a brand new quarter, October 1, you need a compass. You know what provides you the best compass? What can navigate you the best? Last quarter… We all use S&P 500 as our benchmark in this business. Now, the index finished up 2.03% for the third quarter. Not bad, not great… Okay, now how about the worst performers? The ones that really did not help… Then there's a great one, Corning. It fell almost 40%.
Now, this one's misleading because it spiked from $88 at the beginning of the year to $255 at the end of the previous quarter. So, Corning's trip down to $154 last quarter was pure profit-taking. We had a big win in this one for the Charitable Trust because we visited the Corning factory where they make the glass for Apple, Harrodsburg, Kentucky. From that trip, I became certain that fiber is the future of the data center, not copper. So, I'd happily buy this one back if it ever dips again, which it doesn't seem to want to.
Cramer suggested waiting for the stock to fall further in a September episode.
Jim Cramer Says the Chip Shortage “Can’t Be Solved” Without KLAC
Data Center Agreements Support the Fiber Business
Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) has secured several major relationships tied to data center construction. Its multiyear agreement with Meta, announced in January, covers up to $6 billion of optical fiber, cable, and connectivity products. The companies began construction on an expansion of Corning's cable manufacturing operations in North Carolina.
Corning also announced agreements with Amazon and NVIDIA during the second quarter. The NVIDIA partnership calls for a tenfold expansion in Corning's U.S. optical connectivity manufacturing capacity and an increase of more than 50% in domestic fiber production capacity. Amazon's agreement covers optical products for its expanding U.S. data center infrastructure.
Financial performance has improved along with those commitments. Second-quarter core sales rose 17% to approximately $4.74 billion, and core EPS increased 30% to $0.78. Management forecast third-quarter core sales of $4.9 billion to $5 billion and core EPS of $0.85 to $0.89. Core figures are Corning's non-GAAP measures.
Also Check: 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy Under $25
Expansion Requirements And a Rich Earnings Multiple
The agreements require substantial manufacturing expansion. Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) identifies its ability to match capital spending with customer demand, obtain necessary materials and equipment, and manage changes in major-customer orders among its business risks. Its solar manufacturing expansion adds further construction, production-ramp, and profitability requirements.
The quarterly outlook also disappointed investors despite earnings exceeding expectations. Barron's reported that Corning's July results beat forecasts, but its third-quarter guidance largely matched expectations. The shares fell 12% after earnings, showing that the quarter's decline included a reaction to the earnings outlook as well as the profit-taking explanation offered by Cramer.
The company trades at approximately 38.5x forward earnings, which represents a premium to some of its peers including Belden Inc. (BDC) and Amphenol Corporation (APH) that trade at 14.9x and 24.6x, respectively. The businesses are not complete competitors and compete in specific segments with GLW, but the comparison shows that Corning retains a substantial earnings premium despite its retreat from the peak discussed by Cramer. We also discussed another peer of Corning along with the company in a September episode.
Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) appeared in 99 hedge fund portfolios at the end of Q2, up from 91 in the prior quarter, according to Insider Monkey's database tracking more than 1,000 funds. With over 3 million shares, Polar Capital was the most significant hedge fund holder of the company in Q2. The short-interest reading was 2.31% of the public float as of mid-September.
Cramer's willingness to buy another dip is based on fiber demand. Corning's customer agreements support that view, while the scale of its planned manufacturing expansion and its forward earnings premium remain important qualifications.
While we acknowledge the potential of GLW as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Clearing known share supply can lift a stock quickly. Applied Optoelectronics (NASDAQ:AAOI) is showing how after completing its $600 million at-the-market equity program. Applied Optoelectronics stock is at $128.95, up 6% in morning trading. This jump stands out because the…

Clearing known share supply can lift a stock quickly. Applied Optoelectronics (NASDAQ:AAOI) is showing how after completing its $600 million at-the-market equity program. Applied Optoelectronics stock is at $128.95, up 6% in morning trading. This jump stands out because the rest of the optics group is barely moving.
Meanwhile, Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE | LITE Price Prediction) stock is at $1,095.67, up 0.4%, effectively sitting out the rally. Corning (NYSE:GLW) rounds out the group as the glass and fiber maker.
As a gauge of the wider optics group, the Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (CBOE:LYTE) is up 0.42%. For broad-market context, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.43%, leaving the two funds essentially level with each other. That pairing marks the move in Applied Optoelectronics stock as a company-specific adjustment.
Third Share Sale Program of the Year Wraps Up
Applied Optoelectronics announced on Monday the completion of its previously disclosed $600 million at-the-market equity offering program, under which the company sold shares into the open market over time. Founder, president and chief executive Thompson Lin stated that the completion marks the third such program this year and improves the balance sheet of Applied Optoelectronics. Lin added that the program supports the company’s ability to address growing demand for high-speed optical connectivity in AI data centers.
Applied Optoelectronics makes its own optical components and transceivers. It serves AI data center, cable broadband, telecom and fiber-to-the-home customers, with production in Texas, Taiwan and China. That ties output to how fast the company can fund and build capacity, which is why an equity program matters more here than at a larger peer.
Lumentum supplies lasers and optical components at far greater scale, so its growth question centers on order volume, while Corning sits upstream of both as a fiber and glass maker, with exposure to the same data center expansion through a more diversified business.
Roundhill’s fund construction broadens the gap further. The Roundhill fund’s August 6 fact sheet listed Lumentum as its largest holding at 15.4% of net assets, while Applied Optoelectronics carried a 2.1% weight. Such a small slice helps explain why the photonics fund is tracking the S&P 500 even as Applied Optoelectronics stock is soaring.
Completing an at-the-market program removes a known supply of new shares, and the reaction suggests investors saw that drag as the main weight on Applied Optoelectronics stock. The dilution is permanent, while the selling pressure has stopped.
A third equity program in one year is a reminder that Applied Optoelectronics funds its expansion by issuing shares. Both optics names have run hard already, with Applied Optoelectronics stock up 270% year to date and Lumentum stock up 197% over the same stretch. On the bullish side, the fresh capital gives Applied Optoelectronics funding for production equipment aimed at AI connectivity demand.
For Applied Optoelectronics, the key uncertainty is whether funded capacity converts into orders before the next financing arrives. Shareholders may want to monitor any new equity program from the company, given that three have now been completed this year.
Lumentum and Corning offer a broader read on optics demand, and traders may watch whether both names follow Applied Optoelectronics stock higher. Investors weighing their exposure should adjust their holdings carefully given the 270% year-to-date run in Applied Optoelectronics stock and the dilution tied to each new equity program.

Heading into the end of September on a bearish note, shares of Corning (GLW +6.02%) are tumbling lower. With an analyst taking a neutral stance on the tech stock, investors are sensing that today's a good time to click the sell button.

Networking stocks are poised to prosper due to AI spending

According to Thefly.com, Zhu broadly believes that the significant investments companies are making in developing artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure will benefit companies specializing in networking and optical solutions, with demand outpacing supply.
The other catalyst for the tech stock's fall today may simply be that investors are taking profits after Corning stock soared yesterday following news that the company had secured a supply agreement with AT&T worth more than $3 billion.
Is Corning stock a buy on the analyst's bearish outlook?

A leader in manufacturing optical fiber and specialized glass, Corning is at the forefront of providing materials used in various types of today's tech. Potential investors should therefore take the analyst's price target with a grain of salt and weigh the company's financial health more heavily -- a much better indicator of the stock's allure.

Corning Incorporated (ISIN US2193501051) was trading at EUR 146.67 at Lang & Schwarz on October 5, 2026 at 11:01 a.m. CEST, up 0.42 percent versus the prior close of EUR 146.06. On September 29, 2026, Corning signed a multiyear fiber and cable agreement with AT&T valued at more than USD 3.0 billion, according to Corning.
The agreement covers the fiber and cable AT&T needs for network expansion as data and artificial intelligence demand increases. AT&T is targeting 60 million fiber locations by the end of 2030, giving Corning a long-duration demand reference for its Optical Communications business, Reuters reported on September 29, 2026.
The contract follows Corning's second-quarter 2026 report, where core sales increased 17 percent year over year to USD 4.74 billion and core earnings per share rose 30 percent to USD 0.78. The figures came with operating margin of 20.9 percent and free cash flow of USD 1.42 billion, according to the company's earnings-call transcript published by Yahoo Finance.
Optical Communications was the key growth engine in the second quarter of 2026, with sales of USD 2.07 billion, up 32 percent year over year. Enterprise sales increased 65 percent, while artificial-intelligence data-center sales nearly doubled, placing capacity and execution at the center of the next earnings test.
Corning's third-quarter 2026 outlook calls for core sales of USD 4.9 billion to USD 5.0 billion and core earnings per share of USD 0.85 to USD 0.89. Management described the sales range as roughly 16 percent year-over-year growth, while the transcript said enterprise demand remained a significant contributor. The results will be discussed on October 27, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. ET, per Corning's investor calendar.
MarketBeat reported on September 29, 2026, that 18 research firms carried a Moderate Buy consensus, including 12 Buy ratings and six Holds, with an average 12-month target of USD 176.50. The target is a separate U.S.-dollar reference from the euro quote at Lang & Schwarz, so the two prices are not combined.

Corning and AT&T's $3 Billion Fiber Deal Reveals Where AI Spending Goes Next
Corning and AT&T's $3 Billion Fiber Deal Reveals Where AI Spending Goes Next
As AI drives unprecedented data demand, Corning’s $3 billion fiber deal with AT&T highlights the shift from chips to the physical networks that connect them. But soaring growth expectations bring valuation and dilution risks for investors.
Stop typing what you could say in 10 seconds.

The energy story near the Grand Canyon (From Behind the Markets)
Corning and AT&T finalized a multi-year fiber supply deal worth more than $3 billion, reflecting rising demand for optical network infrastructure to support AI and cloud growth.
Corning trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 72 amid heavy insider selling and a planned $2 billion stock offering, raising valuation and dilution concerns despite strong revenue growth.
AT&T is funding a costly network expansion to handle surging data usage, but it offers a lower valuation, a 4.46% dividend yield, and a well-covered payout ratio.
Special Report: Elon Musk’s Hushed FCC Filing. Dec 8th. (From Paradigm Press)
The artificial intelligence (AI) build-out has historically focused on the semiconductor sector, driving valuations to historic premiums as capital chased processing power. However, processing capabilities hold limited utility without the physical infrastructure required to transmit staggering data volumes.
The optical communications supply chain represents the next essential phase of this investment cycle. Corning Incorporated (NYSE: GLW) and AT&T Inc. (NYSE: T) recently finalized a multi-year fiber supply agreement valued at more than $3 billion. This contract marks a transition from speculative hardware multiples to the tangible deployment of next-generation networks. As data consumption surges, securing the physical pathways for cloud and AI integration becomes paramount. Investors evaluating infrastructure plays can look to these developments as a roadmap for where institutional capital is flowing next.
The $100 Stock Behind Elon's Next Move (Ad)
A small, publicly traded supplier trading under $100 a share has reportedly worked alongside Elon Musk for more than a decade.
A federal filing may outline Musk's next major move: an AI network of up to a million satellites powered by the sun. James Altucher says this supplier holds the piece Musk doesn't own.
Watch James Altucher's free Masterclass on this Musk-linked supplier stock
Analyzing the transition from speculative semiconductor multiples to the tangible deployment of next-generation optical networks reveals a changing landscape. Corning operates as a primary bottleneck supplier for telecommunications network expansion and hyperscaler data center infrastructure.
AT&T's recent $3 billion commitment follows a similar multi-billion-dollar fiber supply contract with Verizon (NYSE: VZ) and prior commitments, including a $6 billion agreement with Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) for data center optics.
These supply agreements create a multi-year locked backlog, turning uncertain sector demand into highly visible forward revenue. With multiple major technology and telecommunications entities competing for optical fiber, Corning has consolidated the physical supply chain.
The financial impact of this demand is already materializing in Corning's performance. During the second quarter of 2026, Corning reported a 17.1% year-over-year revenue increase, reaching roughly $4.74 billion. Earnings per share came in at 78 cents, beating consensus estimates of 76 cents. Management projects an annualized sales run rate nearing $20 billion by the end of 2026, scaling toward roughly $40 billion by 2030.
The AT&T deal allows Corning to maximize capacity utilization at its newly announced optical manufacturing plants in North Carolina and Texas. Higher utilization rates and fixed-cost absorption directly catalyze EBITDA margin expansion in the optical communications segment. Expanding these margins creates a clearer pathway to sustained profitability as production scales.
The underlying driver for this infrastructure deployment is an escalating network load. The average AT&T fiber household currently consumes over one terabyte of data monthly, marking a roughly 500% increase since 2016.
AT&T's internal projections point to household consumption reaching roughly 2.0 to 2.5 terabytes per month by 2030. Cloud computing, constant video streaming, and the broad integration of enterprise artificial intelligence tools accelerate this baseline usage.
To support this data density, AT&T has mandated a network expansion to reach 60 million passings by 2030. The recent acquisition of Lumen's mass market fiber business for approximately $5.75 billion requires substantial physical hardware integration to meet these targets. AT&T absorbs the upfront capital expenditure required for this expansion and secures the fiber needed from Corning.
During the second quarter of 2026, AT&T generated roughly $31.56 billion in revenue and reported earnings per share of 65 cents, beating consensus estimates of 59 cents. Carrying this infrastructure load impacts the balance sheet. AT&T's net debt currently sits near 2.68 times EBITDA, slightly above its internal target of 2.5 times. Despite the debt load, AT&T trades at a price-to-earnings ratio near 8.4, paired with a price-to-earnings-growth ratio of approximately 1.26. AT&T maintains an annual dividend payout of $1.11 per share, yielding approximately 4.46%. The payout ratio stands at roughly 36.7% of earnings, suggesting the dividend remains well-covered even amid heavy capital deployment.

Pricing in the Perfection of a Locked Backlog
While Corning's fundamental business benefits from a guaranteed order book, the market has priced in this optimism. Following a notable rally over the past year, Corning trades at a price-to-earnings ratio hovering around 72. This multiple matches or exceeds many pure-play semiconductor and AI hardware manufacturers.
Forward metrics indicate expected earnings growth near 30.5% year over year, which helps contextualize the premium, but the valuation leaves little room for execution errors. Short interest sits at about 17.6 million shares, or roughly 2.1% of the float, reflecting a recent 12% decline as bears cover positions amid strong contract announcements.
Corporate insiders at Corning have executed selling programs throughout the year, suggesting leadership views the current share price as fully valued. Over the trailing 12-month period, insiders liquidated nearly $80 million in equity. Notable transactions include the chief operating officer selling 100,000 shares in June, and an executive vice president offloading 13,100 shares at an average price near $151.29 in August 2026.
Compounding the valuation concerns, Corning filed an at-the-market equity distribution agreement with Goldman Sachs on Sept. 11, 2026, to sell up to $2 billion in new common stock. This filing introduces immediate dilution risk for existing shareholders. Companies often utilize at-the-market offerings to raise capital when they believe their stock commands a market premium. The cash influx will likely fund the manufacturing scale required for the AT&T and Meta contracts, but it requires current investors to accept a smaller slice of future earnings.
Finding the Margin of Safety in AI Infrastructure
Physical fiber deployment is an inescapable prerequisite for the next generation of digital infrastructure. The resulting capital expenditure boom secures Corning's order book and provides exceptional forward revenue visibility that most hardware manufacturers struggle to achieve.
Telecommunications operators like AT&T must upgrade their networks to prevent service degradation and remain competitive, effectively guaranteeing a steady stream of purchase orders for fiber suppliers. Investors evaluating the artificial intelligence and broad connectivity theme face a clear divergence in risk profiles.
The physical hardware supplier offers a high-growth, high-multiple entry point with established dilution risks and heavy insider selling. Conversely, the telecommunications operator absorbs upfront deployment costs but offers a highly compressed valuation multiple and a steady dividend yield. Investors mapping out infrastructure exposure might consider how these distinct profiles fit within a broader portfolio allocation strategy, balancing the supplier's premium growth against the network operator's value-oriented cash flows.

AT&T has broadened its multi-year fiber purchase agreement deal with Corning that is valued at more than $1 billion. The agreement includes Corning's latest 'Evolv' connectivity products. #pressrelease
AT&T (NYSE: T) today announced a multi-year purchase agreement with Corning Incorporated (NYSE: GLW) to provide next-generation fiber, cable, and connectivity solutions to support the expansion of AT&T's fiber network and help bring high-speed internet to more Americans.
AT&T, the largest fiber internet provider in the U.S.*, is expanding its network to bring world-class fiber to more people and places across the country. As Corning's largest customer with preferential volume status for Corning's connectivity solutions, AT&T can accelerate its network expansion and enhance network performance while minimizing deployment costs. The agreement, valued at more than $1 billion, builds on the decades-long collaboration between AT&T and Corning.
AT&T will use the latest additions to Corning's Evolv® portfolio of connectivity solutions, including Evolv® FlexNAP™ with Multifiber Pushlok® Technology, which will be compliant with the Build America, Buy America provisions of the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program (BEAD).
With the best fixed broadband product, AT&T is expanding its network through organic investment, its Gigapower joint venture with BlackRock, and several recently announced commercial open-access agreements. AT&T recently delivered its fifth straight quarter of broadband subscriber growth, passing 28.3M consumer and business locations and remains on pace to pass 30M+ by the end of 2025.

Investors often weigh the stability of an industrial giant against the growth potential of a specialized materials leader. Choosing between Corning (GLW +6.02%) and Honeywell International (HON -0.59%) requires balancing two very different business models.
Corning provides the literal glass and fiber backbone for modern electronics and data centers. Honeywell serves as a massive industrial conglomerate managing everything from airplane cockpits to smart building systems. Both companies are essential to global infrastructure but offer distinct risk and reward profiles.
Corning designs and manufactures specialized glass and optical-physics products. It operates as a vital link for tech stocks by supplying optical fiber to Verizon and durable cover glass to Apple (AAPL +0.22%). The company also partners with Amazon (AMZN +1.95%), Nvidia (NVDA +0.14%), and Qualcomm (QCOM +0.13%) to support artificial intelligence and data center architectures.
Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, particularly in the display and automotive segments. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company reported revenue of nearly $15.6 billion. This represented revenue growth of approximately 19.1% compared to the prior year. Net income reached roughly $1.6 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 10.2% for the period.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.9x. This indicates the company holds roughly $0.90 of debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at 1.6x, meaning it has $1.60 in current assets for every dollar of short-term liabilities. Corning generated nearly $1.4 billion in free cash flow, which is the cash remaining after paying for operations and equipment.
Honeywell International operates as a diversified industrial technology company. It manages four primary segments, including aerospace technologies, industrial automation, and building automation. The company maintains a significant strategic agreement with Bombardier (BDRBF +0.17%) for propulsion and avionics systems. Honeywell is also refining its portfolio by divesting its warehouse and workflow solutions business to focus on higher-growth areas.
In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, Honeywell reported revenue of approximately $37.4 billion. This figure reflected revenue growth of nearly 7.8% over the previous fiscal year. The company achieved a net income of roughly $4.7 billion for the year. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 12.6%, which measures the portion of sales remaining after all expenses are paid.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 2.2x. This indicates that the company's debts are more than double the company's shareholder equity. The current ratio is approximately 1.3x, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term obligations. Honeywell generated close to $5.4 billion in free cash flow, providing significant capital for dividends and acquisitions.
Corning faces risks related to its highly concentrated customer base. A small number of end customers account for more than half of sales in its display and automotive segments. The company also deals with supply chain sensitivities regarding raw materials and energy costs. Geopolitical risks are prominent due to its manufacturing footprint in the Asia Pacific region, which could be impacted by trade policies or tariffs.
Honeywell faces financial exposure from ongoing litigation, such as matters involving Flexjet. The company is currently managing several operational divestitures, which creates execution risk during the portfolio realignment process. Cybersecurity and regulatory compliance also remain critical, especially under rigorous government contracts. Additionally, segments like commercial aviation are subject to cyclicality and fluctuations in broader economic demand.
Honeywell looks cheaper on most metrics, with a lower Forward P/E and a significantly lower P/S ratio.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Corning got its start manufacturing glass for light bulbs, railroad signals, and tableware. Today, its products have a more technology-oriented focus, most notably optical fiber for data transmission. It also makes laboratory products and glass used in electronic device displays. That positions Corning to benefit from the continuing expansion of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data centers, and 5G telecommunications.
But that doesn't make its prospects unbreakable. Corning depends heavily on a relatively small number of large customers, and demand from the technology sector can be cyclical. The company also faces supply chain risks and carries significant debt relative to its shareholders' equity.
Honeywell, meanwhile, produces equipment and software serving four primary markets: aviation, building automation, industrial automation, and energy and sustainability solutions. Its aviation business in particular has provided steady growth and recurring demand. However, aerospace is also cyclical, and Honeywell faces litigation and regulatory risks.
Corning offers greater upside potential from AI infrastructure and the growing demand for optical connectivity, but that opportunity comes with greater risk. Honeywell is far from a perfect investment, but it is the steadier and more defensive choice. Personally, I have considerable confidence in the near-term growth of AI and data-center infrastructure, so Corning is where I would allocate a small, speculative portion of my portfolio.

Can Corning's AT&T Deal Boost Its Optical Communications Growth?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:40 AM PDT 3 min read
Corning Incorporated GLW has secured a multi-year agreement worth more than $3 billion with AT&T Inc. T to expand high-speed broadband infrastructure in the United States. The deal strengthens Corning's position in optical communications as rising data consumption and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption drive greater demand for advanced connectivity.
Under the agreement, Corning will provide the fiber and cable required for AT&T's network expansion, supporting connectivity for residential customers, businesses and communities. Its fiber and connectivity solutions are expected to accelerate network deployment, improve installation efficiency and support the domestic connectivity supply chain.
Corning is also expanding its fiber and cable production in the United States, including a North Carolina facility that has created hundreds of jobs. These investments will increase the company's manufacturing capacity and strengthen its ability to supply fiber solutions for next-generation network infrastructure.
Corning has also partnered with Verizon Communications Inc. VZ to provide fiber and connectivity solutions for broadband expansion and AI-related infrastructure. As telecom companies continue to invest in higher-capacity networks, Corning is likely to benefit from sustained demand for optical fiber and related solutions, supporting its growth opportunities in the communications market.
How Are Competitors Focusing on Fiber?
Corning faces competition from Amphenol Corporation APH and Lumen Technologies, Inc. LUMN. Amphenol is strengthening its fiber-optic capabilities to meet growing demand from data centers and AI applications. The company is seeing strong demand for fiber-based connectivity as customers upgrade networks to support higher data speeds and capacity. Amphenol's expanding portfolio of fiber-optic and interconnect products helps meet the growing need for reliable, high-speed data transmission.
Lumen is adding new fiber routes and network capacity as AI workloads drive greater data traffic across the United States. Its NorthLine project will connect Seattle and Minneapolis through a low-latency route designed to support high-capacity data movement between data centers and cloud networks. Lumen is expanding its network infrastructure to meet the growing connectivity needs of businesses, data centers and AI applications.
Corning's Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Shares of Corning have rallied 85.0% over the past year compared with the industry's growth of 130.4%.
From a valuation standpoint, the company's shares currently trade at 38.14 forward 12-month earnings, higher than the industry tally of 35.07.
Corning's earnings estimates for 2026 have increased 0.9% to $3.28 per share, while the same for 2027 have risen 0.7% to $4.28 over the past 60 days.

A major deal with a top name in the telecom sphere propelled Corning (GLW +6.02%) stock to a solid gain on Tuesday. It did not get more specific about the contract's value or length.

"This means more access to the connectivity they need today, tomorrow, and for generations to come," it added.

On September 9, 2026, Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI | ADI Price Prediction) said it will acquire Alif Semiconductor, a builder of AI-native microcontrollers, for cash plus up to $200 million in performance-based payments.
Alif’s chips let a device interpret motion, sound and vibration locally, without a cloud round trip. Bolted onto ADI’s sensing, signal processing and power franchises, the stack looks like a nervous system for factory robots, medical devices and defense platforms.
The strategic logic is straightforward: as machine intelligence leaves the data center, ADI owns the physical interface. But the headline question deserves a straight answer. ADI is going after a different market than NVIDIA training GPUs, one with different economics (we reverse-engineered what the biggest tech winners looked like early in a free playbook here), and the Alif deal is the clearest statement yet of that ambition.
Shares trade at $365.07, up 48.95% over the past year.
A microcontroller is a small computer embedded inside equipment. Sensor fusion means combining several imperfect signals, say a gyroscope and an accelerometer, into one usable reading.
Inference at the edge means the decision happens on the device itself. A robot arm cannot wait for a data-center round trip, and a pacemaker cannot depend on Wi-Fi.
Latency, bandwidth cost, power budget, and reliability when connectivity drops are the physical reasons edge inference exists. Alif’s parts fold neural-network execution into that footprint.
Wrap that around ADI’s converters, amplifiers, and power management, and one supplier can sell the whole sensing-to-decision loop.
Edge Inference Versus Data-Center Training
Training a frontier model requires tens of thousands of GPUs in a hyperscale hall, a workload well outside Alif’s design point and outside ADI’s stated ambition.
CEO Vincent Roche framed the target directly: “AI extends its reach from the data center to the physical world in the form of pervasive robotics, digital health, autonomous mobility.”
ADI’s data-center exposure is real and growing, with communications up 84% year over year in the July quarter. But that revenue comes from power delivery, optical control, and timing around GPUs, not from replacing them.
Edge inference is a separate market because the constraints are opposite: microwatts, not megawatts, and unit volumes measured in billions of embedded devices.
ADI produced $13.88 billion in trailing revenue and carries a $175.99 billion market cap. A tuck-in has to compound for years to move that needle.
Industrial and medical qualification cycles run long, often two to four years before a design win ships in volume. Alif competitors include STMicro, NXP, Renesas and Ambiq, all fighting for the same sockets.
Integration risk is real, and ADI is still absorbing Empower Semiconductor, the $1.5 billion power-management deal that closed in July.
The forward multiple sits at 22x against an analyst target of $470.25, with 31 buy or strong-buy ratings versus 3 holds.
Fiscal Q4 guidance calls for $4.3 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $3.86, a genuine record.
Alif deepens a credible edge-AI franchise on top of a business already compounding at 39.6% revenue growth. The setup looks credible, though it would weaken if the Empower ramp stalls or a data-center capex pause exposes the multiple.

The end of the earnings season is always a good time to take a step back and see who shined (and who didn't). Let's take a look at how analog semiconductors stocks fared in Q2, starting with Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI).
Demand for analog chips is generally linked to the overall level of economic growth, as analog chips serve as the building blocks of most electronic goods and equipment. Unlike digital chip designers, analog chip makers tend to produce the majority of their own chips, as analog chip production does not require expensive leading edge nodes. Less dependent on major secular growth drivers, analog product cycles are much longer, often 5-7 years.
The 14 analog semiconductors stocks we track reported a very strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 1.8% while next quarter's revenue guidance was 4.9% above.

Founded by two MIT graduates, Ray Stata and Matthew Lorber in 1965, Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI) is one of the largest providers of high performance analog integrated circuits used mainly in industrial end markets, along with communications, autos, and consumer devices.
Analog Devices reported revenues of $4.02 billion, up 39.6% year on year. This print exceeded analysts' expectations by 2.6%. "ADI delivered a strong third quarter, exceeding the midpoint of our revenue, margin, and earnings outlook as we capitalized on broad-based demand," said Vincent Roche, CEO and Chair.

MCHP Expands Ethernet Portfolio: Can it Challenge TXN & ADI?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:20 AM PDT 4 min read
Microchip Technology MCHP has expanded its 10BASE-T1S Single Pair Ethernet portfolio with the launch of the LAN8679 and LAN8680 PMD transceivers and the LAN8660X/1X/2X endpoint family with integrated transceivers. The products are designed for next-generation zonal architectures across automotive, industrial, robotics and aerospace and defense applications, extending Ethernet connectivity to edge nodes while reducing wiring and system complexity. The portfolio combines transceivers, endpoint functionality, power management and embedded-control capabilities, thereby supporting MCHP's broader Total System Solutions strategy. It also improves competitive prowess against the likes of Texas Instruments TXN and Analog Devices ADI.
The LAN8679 features an Open Alliance 3-Pin interface in a compact package, while the LAN8680 adds power management, wake as well as sleep control and watchdog supervision. The LAN8660X/1X/2X family integrates a transceiver into a single-chip Remote Control Protocol solution, eliminating the need for external PHY components in applications such as control systems, lighting and audio. Microchip's 10BASE-T1S multidrop architecture can connect eight or more nodes over a single bus, helping reduce wiring weight, costs and gateway requirements.
The portfolio expansion strengthens Microchip's connectivity and networking growth strategy. The company identifies connectivity/networking as one of its new strategic growth pillars, targeting opportunities across Industry 4.0, automotive and data-center applications. MCHP highlights Single Pair Ethernet as a roughly $4-billion served available market, spanning automotive, aerospace, robotics, industrial vehicles, building controls, industrial controls, sensors, actuators and vehicle networking. The company also sees billions of legacy nodes as potential replacement opportunities, giving the expanded portfolio a sizable long-term addressable market.
The launch is also well timed with improving demand in MCHP's two largest target markets for these products. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, industrial represented 32.2% of revenues and automotive accounted for 15%. Industrial revenues increased 24.3% year over year, while automotive revenues jumped 29.3%. Industrial and automotive customers had largely completed inventory corrections, and Microchip noted that clients were placing a higher number of orders, while bookings remained strong across product lines, business units and geographies. The new devices are expected to help Microchip capture more semiconductor content as automotive and industrial networks migrate from fragmented legacy architectures toward consolidated Ethernet-based systems.
Texas Instruments' DP83TD555 targets 10BASE-T1S connectivity, while ADI's AD3300/AD3301 family brings integrated Ethernet connectivity to edge sensors and actuators.
Texas Instruments is challenging Microchip across automotive and industrial connectivity through its broad Analog and Embedded Processing portfolio, strong manufacturing capacity and growing semiconductor content per system. In the second quarter of 2026, TXN's industrial revenues increased roughly 30% year over year, while automotive revenues rose in the mid-teens. Texas Instruments' supply capabilities further intensify the challenge. The company has available clean-room space and is expanding production capacity to address rising demand.
Analog Devices poses a significant challenge through its high-performance analog, sensing, power and embedded technologies. Industrial accounted for 49% of ADI's third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues and increased 53% year over year, led partly by automation, while automotive represented 25% of revenues and grew 16%. ADI said its higher content and share positions are driving automotive growth across next-generation ADAS, infotainment and electric powertrains. ADI is also positioning for the emergence of physical AI, including robotics and autonomous mobility.

Analog Devices to acquire Alif Semiconductor in $1.3bn cash deal
Alif Semiconductor to be acquired by Analog Devices. · Verdict · JHVEPhoto/Shutterstock.com.
US-based semiconductor company Analog Devices (ADI) has reached an agreement to acquire Alif Semiconductor in an all-cash transaction valued at $1.35bn.
The deal is expected to strengthen Analog Devices' position in providing hardware for AI applications in real-world systems.
The agreement also entails a potential additional payment of up to $200m, depending on certain undisclosed conditions.
Based in California, Alif Semiconductor currently supplies silicon to a range of consumer and industrial customers, with its products already shipping in production.
The company has developed a platform of AI-native microcontrollers and fusion processors, featuring a heterogeneous architecture designed to enable real-time sensor fusion, low-latency inference, and on-device AI processing.
Alif Semiconductor co-founder and president Reza Kazerounian said: "Alif was founded to reimagine what a microcontroller can be in the AI era. We engineered a heterogeneous architecture from the start, integrating dedicated low-power neural processing with connectivity, security, and intelligent power management that delivers compute resources precisely where they're needed.
"Combined with ADI's deep physical-domain expertise and broad analog system capabilities, we can expand our reach to deliver the solutions that can power the future of Physical Intelligence."
Through the acquisition, Analog Devices aims to address an expanded range of applications, including industrial, defence, data centre infrastructure, digital health, robotics, energy, and wearable devices. It plans to achieve this by combining its sensor, power, and software capabilities with Alif Semiconductor's AI-native processing platform.
Analog Devices CEO and chair Vincent Roche said: "By combining Alif's digital processing capabilities with our leadership in multi-modal sensing, signal processing, power, connectivity, and software, we can empower customers to create entirely new classes of secure, intelligent systems that sense, reason, and act locally in real time.
"This is the next frontier of AI: embodied and deterministic. This is Physical Intelligence in action."
The companies anticipate the transaction will be completed by the end of this year, pending customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. This includes the expiration of any applicable waiting periods under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act.
In May, Analog Devices announced to acquire Empower Semiconductor, a Silicon Valley company, in a cash deal valued at approximately $1.5bn. Analog Devices completed the acquisition in July 2026.

Analog Devices Wants Robots to Think Without Nvidia | Is ADI the Next Big AI Stock?
Analog Devices just spent up to $200 million to put AI decision-making inside robots and pacemakers, bypassing the cloud entirely. Whether that bet makes ADI the next great AI hardware winner depends on a market most investors have never thought…
Published September 10, 2026, 1:30pm ET · 3 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Tesla's Optimus robots are envisioned to revolutionize manufacturing, seen here working diligently on an assembly line. However, the advanced dexterity required for complex tasks remains a key challenge in achieving mass production goals. © Shutterstock
On September 9, 2026, Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI | ADI Price Prediction) said it will acquire Alif Semiconductor, a builder of AI-native microcontrollers, for cash plus up to $200 million in performance-based payments.
Alif’s chips let a device interpret motion, sound and vibration locally, without a cloud round trip. Bolted onto ADI’s sensing, signal processing and power franchises, the stack looks like a nervous system for factory robots, medical devices and defense platforms.
The strategic logic is straightforward: as machine intelligence leaves the data center, ADI owns the physical interface. But the headline question deserves a straight answer. ADI is going after a different market than NVIDIA training GPUs, one with different economics (we reverse-engineered what the biggest tech winners looked like early in a free playbook here), and the Alif deal is the clearest statement yet of that ambition.
Shares trade at $365.07, up 48.95% over the past year.
A microcontroller is a small computer embedded inside equipment. Sensor fusion means combining several imperfect signals, say a gyroscope and an accelerometer, into one usable reading.
Inference at the edge means the decision happens on the device itself. A robot arm cannot wait for a data-center round trip, and a pacemaker cannot depend on Wi-Fi.
Latency, bandwidth cost, power budget, and reliability when connectivity drops are the physical reasons edge inference exists. Alif’s parts fold neural-network execution into that footprint.
Wrap that around ADI’s converters, amplifiers, and power management, and one supplier can sell the whole sensing-to-decision loop.
Edge Inference Versus Data-Center Training
Training a frontier model requires tens of thousands of GPUs in a hyperscale hall, a workload well outside Alif’s design point and outside ADI’s stated ambition.
CEO Vincent Roche framed the target directly: “AI extends its reach from the data center to the physical world in the form of pervasive robotics, digital health, autonomous mobility.”
ADI’s data-center exposure is real and growing, with communications up 84% year over year in the July quarter. But that revenue comes from power delivery, optical control, and timing around GPUs, not from replacing them.
Edge inference is a separate market because the constraints are opposite: microwatts, not megawatts, and unit volumes measured in billions of embedded devices.
ADI produced $13.88 billion in trailing revenue and carries a $175.99 billion market cap. A tuck-in has to compound for years to move that needle.
Industrial and medical qualification cycles run long, often two to four years before a design win ships in volume. Alif competitors include STMicro, NXP, Renesas and Ambiq, all fighting for the same sockets.
Integration risk is real, and ADI is still absorbing Empower Semiconductor, the $1.5 billion power-management deal that closed in July.
The forward multiple sits at 22x against an analyst target of $470.25, with 31 buy or strong-buy ratings versus 3 holds.
Fiscal Q4 guidance calls for $4.3 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $3.86, a genuine record.
Alif deepens a credible edge-AI franchise on top of a business already compounding at 39.6% revenue growth. The setup looks credible, though it would weaken if the Empower ramp stalls or a data-center capex pause exposes the multiple.

Analog Semiconductors Stocks Q2 Recap: Benchmarking Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI)
The end of the earnings season is always a good time to take a step back and see who shined (and who didn't). Let's take a look at how analog semiconductors stocks fared in Q2, starting with Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI).
Demand for analog chips is generally linked to the overall level of economic growth, as analog chips serve as the building blocks of most electronic goods and equipment. Unlike digital chip designers, analog chip makers tend to produce the majority of their own chips, as analog chip production does not require expensive leading edge nodes. Less dependent on major secular growth drivers, analog product cycles are much longer, often 5-7 years.
The 14 analog semiconductors stocks we track reported a very strong Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 1.8% while next quarter's revenue guidance was 4.9% above.
In light of this news, share prices of the companies have held steady as they are up 2.2% on average since the latest earnings results.
Founded by two MIT graduates, Ray Stata and Matthew Lorber in 1965, Analog Devices (NASDAQ:ADI) is one of the largest providers of high performance analog integrated circuits used mainly in industrial end markets, along with communications, autos, and consumer devices.
Analog Devices reported revenues of $4.02 billion, up 39.6% year on year. This print exceeded analysts' expectations by 2.6%. Overall, it was a very strong quarter for the company with revenue guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations and an impressive beat of analysts' operating income estimates.
"ADI delivered a strong third quarter, exceeding the midpoint of our revenue, margin, and earnings outlook as we capitalized on broad-based demand," said Vincent Roche, CEO and Chair.
Interestingly, the stock is up 6% since reporting and currently trades at $399.13.
Is now the time to buy Analog Devices? Access our full analysis of the earnings results here, it's free.
Best Q2: Monolithic Power Systems (NASDAQ:MPWR)
Founded in 1997 by its longtime CEO Michael Hsing, Monolithic Power Systems (NASDAQ:MPWR) is an analog and mixed signal chipmaker that specializes in power management chips meant to minimize total energy consumption.
Monolithic Power Systems reported revenues of $980.6 million, up 47.6% year on year, outperforming analysts' expectations by 8.6%. The business had an incredible quarter with a significant improvement in its inventory levels and a beat of analysts' EPS estimates.
Monolithic Power Systems scored the biggest analyst estimate beat, highest guidance raise, and fastest revenue growth of the whole group. The market seems content with the results as the stock is up 2.8% since reporting. It currently trades at $1,353.
Is now the time to buy Monolithic Power Systems? Access our full analysis of the earnings results here, it's free.
Taiwan-based Himax Technologies (NASDAQ:HIMX) is a leading manufacturer of display driver chips and timing controllers used in TVs, laptops, and mobile phones.
Himax reported revenues of $227.4 million, up 5.9% year on year, exceeding analysts' expectations by 2%. Still, it was a slower quarter as it posted EPS in line with analysts' estimates.
Interestingly, the stock is up 5.7% since the results and currently trades at $14.11.
Read our full analysis of Himax's results here.
Founded by Caltech professor Carver Mead and one of his students Chris Diorio, Impinj (NASDAQ:PI) is a maker of radio-frequency identification (RFID) hardware and software.
Impinj reported revenues of $108.4 million, up 10.7% year on year. This print topped analysts' expectations by 3.5%. Overall, it was a stunning quarter as it also produced a significant improvement in its inventory levels and a beat of analysts' EPS estimates.
The stock is up 28.7% since reporting and currently trades at $179.28.
Read our full, actionable report on Impinj here, it's free.
Founded in the 1950s as Microwave Associates, a communications supplier to the US Army Signal Corp, today MACOM Technology Solutions (NASDAQ: MTSI) is a provider of analog chips used in optical, wireless, and satellite networks.
MACOM reported revenues of $342.2 million, up 35.8% year on year. This number surpassed analysts' expectations by 1.9%. It was a very strong quarter as it also put up revenue guidance for next quarter exceeding analysts' expectations and a solid beat of analysts' operating income estimates.
The stock is up 9.5% since reporting and currently trades at $288.49.
Read our full, actionable report on MACOM here, it's free.
Over the past year, investors have been forced to repeatedly answer the same question: what is the market's biggest risk? The answer has changed several times, and each shift has reshaped market leadership.
Late in 2025 and early 2026, artificial intelligence became the market's primary uncertainty. Investors questioned whether AI would erode software pricing power and weaken competitive moats as AI made it easier to replicate once-differentiated products.
By the spring, technology took a back seat to geopolitics. The U.S. conflict with Iran briefly became the market's dominant narrative, raising concerns about oil prices, inflation, and global growth. But as energy markets remained orderly and fears of a prolonged supply disruption faded, investors quickly turned their focus back to fundamentals.

Analog Devices stock (ISIN US0326541051) is drawing renewed attention after the company issued USD 3 billion in senior notes on September 17, 2026, adding leverage on the heels of strong fiscal third quarter growth in its industrial business as of fiscal 2026.
Debt issuance adds leverage after strong Q3
According to GuruFocus on September 18, 2026, Analog Devices issued USD 3.0 billion in aggregate principal amount of senior notes across four tranches on September 17, 2026, including USD 500 million notes due September 15, 2029, USD 500 million notes due October 1, 2031, and two USD 1 billion tranches due October 1, 2033 and October 1, 2036.
The same overview notes that GuruFocus estimates a fair value for Analog Devices shares near USD 337.27 using its GF Value model, suggesting the stock is about 7.5 percent overvalued at that level compared with its intrinsic value estimate, and that roughly 20 institutional investors described as gurus currently hold the stock with a mix of additions and trims in recent quarters.
Industrial and automotive drive fiscal Q3 momentum
A recent analysis from Zacks on September 17, 2026, highlights that Analog Devices industrial revenues reached USD 1.97 billion in fiscal third quarter 2026, up 53 percent year over year and 10 percent sequentially, representing 49 percent of total company revenue in that period.
The same Zacks piece states that the strength in industrial, automotive and communications end markets helped drive overall revenue growth in fiscal Q3 2026, and it notes that the Zacks consensus estimate for Analog Devices fiscal 2026 earnings implies year over year earnings growth of 66.4 percent compared with the prior fiscal year.
According to the consensus cited by Zacks, estimates for fiscal 2026 earnings have been revised upward over the past 30 days as analysts factor in the stronger margin profile and demand trends in industrial and automotive segments.
Analyst views and longer term earnings potential
On the analyst side, Investing.com reported on September 17, 2026 that Cantor Fitzgerald reiterated an Overweight rating on Analog Devices shares with a price target of USD 550, highlighting potential upside scenarios for earnings per share into fiscal 2028 compared with current levels.
The broader qualitative context is that, as Ground News summarized on September 18, 2026, Analog Devices fiscal Q3 results show that demand for its analog and mixed signal chips is being driven not only by artificial intelligence infrastructure but also by traditional industrial automation and automotive applications.
Per recent market commentary on September 18, 2026, semiconductor stocks have led broader US equity gains, with sector indices such as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rising more than 3 percent, which provides a supportive backdrop for Analog Devices stock despite the incremental leverage from the USD 3.0 billion note issuance.

Analog Devices, AMD, KLA Corporation, Lam Research, and Marvell Technology Stocks Trade Up, What You Need To Know
What Happened?
A number of stocks jumped in the afternoon session after weaker-than-expected U.S. employment data cooled Treasury yields, easing interest rate pressure.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm payrolls increased by 29,000 in September, falling short of the 84,000 projected by economists polled by Dow Jones, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%.For the broader group, softer hiring eases interest-rate pressure on high-multiple growth equities by pulling borrowing costs lower.
However, further deceleration in the labor market risks dampening cyclical end-market demand across industrial and automotive chip channels.Semiconductor valuations expand when falling yields reduce the discount rate on long-duration earnings, provided enterprise infrastructure spending does not deteriorate.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

The previous big move we wrote about was 28 days ago when the stock gained 7.2% on the news that investors shrugged off interest rate hike expectations following the August jobs report and unwound defensive positioning in beaten-down chip designers, according to Bloomberg.
The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employers added 162,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in August, easily beating estimates of a 56,000 increase from economists polled by FactSet. The agency also reported that the national unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%.The strong labor data initially raised expectations for further monetary tightening, but odds of a September quarter-point interest rate hike settled at a coin-toss 50%, according to federal funds futures data reported by Bloomberg.
Typically, higher interest rates place downward pressure on high-growth technology equities by discounting future projected cash flows.Despite these macroeconomic concerns, traders rotated back into the chip sector. During the regular session, KLA Corporation rose 7.98% and Semtech climbed 7.96%, while Marvell Technology advanced 5.92% and Advanced Micro Devices gained 4.18%, according to stock market quote data.

MCHP Expands Ethernet Portfolio: Can it Challenge TXN & ADI?
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 6:20 AM PDT 4 min read
Microchip Technology MCHP has expanded its 10BASE-T1S Single Pair Ethernet portfolio with the launch of the LAN8679 and LAN8680 PMD transceivers and the LAN8660X/1X/2X endpoint family with integrated transceivers. The products are designed for next-generation zonal architectures across automotive, industrial, robotics and aerospace and defense applications, extending Ethernet connectivity to edge nodes while reducing wiring and system complexity. The portfolio combines transceivers, endpoint functionality, power management and embedded-control capabilities, thereby supporting MCHP's broader Total System Solutions strategy. It also improves competitive prowess against the likes of Texas Instruments TXN and Analog Devices ADI.
The LAN8679 features an Open Alliance 3-Pin interface in a compact package, while the LAN8680 adds power management, wake as well as sleep control and watchdog supervision. The LAN8660X/1X/2X family integrates a transceiver into a single-chip Remote Control Protocol solution, eliminating the need for external PHY components in applications such as control systems, lighting and audio. Microchip's 10BASE-T1S multidrop architecture can connect eight or more nodes over a single bus, helping reduce wiring weight, costs and gateway requirements.
The portfolio expansion strengthens Microchip's connectivity and networking growth strategy. The company identifies connectivity/networking as one of its new strategic growth pillars, targeting opportunities across Industry 4.0, automotive and data-center applications. MCHP highlights Single Pair Ethernet as a roughly $4-billion served available market, spanning automotive, aerospace, robotics, industrial vehicles, building controls, industrial controls, sensors, actuators and vehicle networking. The company also sees billions of legacy nodes as potential replacement opportunities, giving the expanded portfolio a sizable long-term addressable market.
The launch is also well timed with improving demand in MCHP's two largest target markets for these products. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, industrial represented 32.2% of revenues and automotive accounted for 15%. Industrial revenues increased 24.3% year over year, while automotive revenues jumped 29.3%. Industrial and automotive customers had largely completed inventory corrections, and Microchip noted that clients were placing a higher number of orders, while bookings remained strong across product lines, business units and geographies. The new devices are expected to help Microchip capture more semiconductor content as automotive and industrial networks migrate from fragmented legacy architectures toward consolidated Ethernet-based systems.
Texas Instruments' DP83TD555 targets 10BASE-T1S connectivity, while ADI's AD3300/AD3301 family brings integrated Ethernet connectivity to edge sensors and actuators.
Texas Instruments is challenging Microchip across automotive and industrial connectivity through its broad Analog and Embedded Processing portfolio, strong manufacturing capacity and growing semiconductor content per system. In the second quarter of 2026, TXN's industrial revenues increased roughly 30% year over year, while automotive revenues rose in the mid-teens. Texas Instruments' supply capabilities further intensify the challenge. The company has available clean-room space and is expanding production capacity to address rising demand.
Analog Devices poses a significant challenge through its high-performance analog, sensing, power and embedded technologies. Industrial accounted for 49% of ADI's third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues and increased 53% year over year, led partly by automation, while automotive represented 25% of revenues and grew 16%. ADI said its higher content and share positions are driving automotive growth across next-generation ADAS, infotainment and electric powertrains. ADI is also positioning for the emergence of physical AI, including robotics and autonomous mobility.
MCHP's Share Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Shares of Microchip have appreciated 22% year to date, outperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's rise of 21.8%.
The MCHP stock is trading at a premium, with a trailing price/book multiple of 6.55 compared with the Zacks Semiconductor – Analog and Mixed industry's 6.48. Microchip has a Value Score of D.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Microchip's fiscal 2027 earnings is currently pegged at $3.63 per share, up 15.6% over the past 30 days, suggesting 121.3% growth from fiscal 2026's reported figure.

This fresh debt financing comes as Analog Devices reports very large year-over-year gains in revenue and earnings, supported by improving industrial demand and growing AI-related data center activity.
With this combination of new long-term debt and AI-driven business momentum, we'll explore how the financing shapes Analog Devices' investment narrative.

What Is Analog Devices' Investment Narrative?
To own Analog Devices, you need to believe in its role as a core supplier to industrial, automotive, and data center customers, especially as AI drives more complex sensing and power needs. The recent US$4.0 billions senior notes issue adds long-dated, unsecured funding on top of strong recent revenue and earnings gains, and looks more like balance-sheet housekeeping than a swing factor for near-term results. The main short term catalysts still sit in industrial recovery, AI-related data center demand, and the company's ability to sustain high margins while supporting a growing dividend and active buybacks. The new debt nudges financial risk higher via interest costs, but also gives management extra flexibility if conditions tighten, so it slightly reframes, rather than redefines, the risk-reward trade off.

Analog Devices to acquire Alif Semiconductor in $1.3bn cash deal
Alif Semiconductor to be acquired by Analog Devices. · Verdict · JHVEPhoto/Shutterstock.com.
US-based semiconductor company Analog Devices (ADI) has reached an agreement to acquire Alif Semiconductor in an all-cash transaction valued at $1.35bn.
The deal is expected to strengthen Analog Devices' position in providing hardware for AI applications in real-world systems.
The agreement also entails a potential additional payment of up to $200m, depending on certain undisclosed conditions.
Based in California, Alif Semiconductor currently supplies silicon to a range of consumer and industrial customers, with its products already shipping in production.
The company has developed a platform of AI-native microcontrollers and fusion processors, featuring a heterogeneous architecture designed to enable real-time sensor fusion, low-latency inference, and on-device AI processing.
Alif Semiconductor co-founder and president Reza Kazerounian said: "Alif was founded to reimagine what a microcontroller can be in the AI era. We engineered a heterogeneous architecture from the start, integrating dedicated low-power neural processing with connectivity, security, and intelligent power management that delivers compute resources precisely where they're needed.
"Combined with ADI's deep physical-domain expertise and broad analog system capabilities, we can expand our reach to deliver the solutions that can power the future of Physical Intelligence."
Through the acquisition, Analog Devices aims to address an expanded range of applications, including industrial, defence, data centre infrastructure, digital health, robotics, energy, and wearable devices. It plans to achieve this by combining its sensor, power, and software capabilities with Alif Semiconductor's AI-native processing platform.
Analog Devices CEO and chair Vincent Roche said: "By combining Alif's digital processing capabilities with our leadership in multi-modal sensing, signal processing, power, connectivity, and software, we can empower customers to create entirely new classes of secure, intelligent systems that sense, reason, and act locally in real time.
"This is the next frontier of AI: embodied and deterministic. This is Physical Intelligence in action."
The companies anticipate the transaction will be completed by the end of this year, pending customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. This includes the expiration of any applicable waiting periods under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act.
In May, Analog Devices announced to acquire Empower Semiconductor, a Silicon Valley company, in a cash deal valued at approximately $1.5bn. Analog Devices completed the acquisition in July 2026.
"Analog Devices to acquire Alif Semiconductor in $1.3bn cash deal" was originally created and published by Verdict, a GlobalData owned brand.
